waves.title: How Airports Make Money: Aeronautical and Non-Aeronautical Revenue Explained
waves.keywords: how do airports make money, airport revenue model, aeronautical revenue, non-aeronautical revenue airports, airport business model
waves.brief: The title's position piece and the most winnable pillar query in the vertical: the current SERP is a university's content-marketing page, Quora, an ETF provider's blog and one vendor (TAV Technologies) — no trade publisher ranks at all. Write the definitive operator-side explainer. Structure: what aeronautical revenue is (landing and passenger charges, and why regulators cap them), what non-aeronautical revenue is, and the split — per ACI World's Airport Economics Report, global airport industry revenue was 194.9 billion dollars in 2024, roughly 54 percent aeronautical and 37 percent non-aeronautical, with non-aero at 73.3 billion dollars and forecast by ACI to reach 99 billion by 2033; attribute every figure to ACI and the year. Break down the non-aero lines with the ACI splits: parking is 24.1 percent of global non-aero revenue and 43.2 percent in North America, where it is the single biggest commercial line; retail leads in Europe at 26.7 percent. Explain why non-aero is the margin story: regulated aero charges versus commercial income, and quote ACI's 2024 global airport ROIC of 6.3 percent to show how thin the overall return is. Cover the main levers one by one: duty free and retail concessions (minimum annual guarantee versus revenue-share models), F&B, car parking and drop-off charges, advertising concessions, property and cargo, and route incentives as a cost of growing the aero side. A comparison table of revenue lines with the model, the margin character and who operates it. FAQ: is duty free the airport's own shop (usually a concessionaire), why is airport parking so expensive (it is a yield-managed revenue line), do airlines pay to use airports. Never assert a market size in our own voice; the scope-and-figure rule applies throughout. SOURCE ANCHORS (all pre-verified 24 Aug 2026 — cite in text, do not re-derive): non-aero was 73.3 billion dollars of 194.9 billion total in 2024, which is 37.6 percent — write 'around 38 percent' or 'just over a third', never pair '37 percent' with the 73.3 figure or the arithmetic reads wrong. Avolta lineage is fact: Dufry acquired World Duty Free in 2015 and rebranded as Avolta in 2023 after combining with Autogrill, so World Duty Free is an Avolta brand, not a separate operator — state the lineage in one line. SSP Group's website is foodtravelexperts.com.

waves.title: How Much Does It Cost to Build an Airport? Real Project Data from 20 Live Builds
waves.keywords: how much does it cost to build an airport, airport construction cost, cost of building a runway, new airport cost, airport terminal construction cost
waves.brief: The weakest SERP measured in the vertical research: Medium posts, Quora, Scribd, cost-guide content farms and one stale 2021 trade listicle. Displace it with real, sourced project data. Anchor the piece in a table of live and recent projects with their published costs, each attributed to the promoter or a named report and dated: Western Sydney (5.3 billion Australian dollars, opened on budget 2026, Bechtel delivery), Noida Jewar phase 1 (around 11,200 crore rupees, opened 2026, Zurich Airport AG), Navi Mumbai (over 2 billion dollars, Adani, opened 2025), Gatwick northern runway (2.2 billion pounds, privately financed), Dublin infrastructure plan (2 billion euros), Manchester transformation (1.3 billion pounds), Changi T5 (around 10 billion dollars), JFK redevelopment (19 billion dollars), O'Hare (approved at 8.5 billion dollars in 2018, now around 12 billion in current dollars — use this pair to explain escalation), LAX (30 billion dollars), Dubai Al Maktoum (35 billion dollars), Riyadh King Salman (30 billion dollars core, with programme figures up to 100 billion circulating — quote the range and explain the scope difference per the scope-and-figure rule), Heathrow third runway (49 billion pounds programme: 21 billion runway, 12 billion terminals and M25 works, 15 billion campus modernisation). Then explain what drives the spread: greenfield versus expansion, runways versus terminals (a runway is civil engineering, a terminal is a building with baggage, screening and IT systems inside), land and airspace, the people-mover and ground-transport layer, and why megaproject budgets escalate. Close with the honest per-unit rules of thumb the industry uses, always as attributed ranges, never our own estimate. SOURCE ANCHORS (all pre-verified 24 Aug 2026 — attribute these in text exactly, they are newer than the model's memory): Heathrow's 49 billion pound figure is the TOTAL programme cost reported by Bloomberg on 24 Nov 2025 when ministers backed the scheme (21 billion runway, 12 billion terminals and M25 works, 15 billion campus modernisation) — older 14 to 33 billion figures referred to the runway element alone, and the article should say so rather than quoting 49 billion bare. Changi T5 has no official published total; reported figures are in Singapore dollars, at least S$10 billion — never state a US dollar figure. Navi Mumbai: inaugurated 8 Oct 2025, commercial operations began 25 Dec 2025 (Adani) — use both dates, do not say 'opened 2025' bare. Noida Jewar phase 1: quote as 'around 10,000 to 11,200 crore rupees, per Yamuna International Airport reporting' — a range, attributed. Western Sydney: A$5.3bn, delivery phase reported on budget by Bechtel, passenger opening 25 Oct 2026 — phrase as 'reported on budget ahead of opening', not as a completed verdict. Riyadh King Salman: masterplan is SIX parallel runways per KSIADC/Foster + Partners announcements — attribute to the masterplan, not asserted bare. STRUCTURAL REQUIREMENTS: the exact phrase 'cost to build an airport' must appear in the first paragraph. EVERY row of the project table carries its dated source in the row itself — Heathrow (Bloomberg, Nov 2025), Gatwick (DfT approval Sep 2025, Court of Appeal Aug 2026), Dubai Al Maktoum $35bn (Dubai Media Office announcement, Apr 2024), LAX $30bn (LAWA programme figures), Riyadh $30bn core (KSIADC), Western Sydney A$5.3bn and 25 Oct 2026 passenger opening (WSI/Bechtel announcements, 2026), Navi Mumbai (Adani: inaugurated 8 Oct 2025, commercial ops 25 Dec 2025), Noida Jewar (YIAPL: inaugurated 28 Mar 2026, commercial ops from 15 Jun 2026), Changi T5 (CAG/MOT Singapore, ground broken May 2025), JFK $19bn (Port Authority), O'Hare (Chicago Dept of Aviation, ~$12bn current dollars). These dates and attributions are pre-verified editorial fact supplied by the commissioning research — the article's job is to carry them with their attributions, not to re-verify them.

waves.title: Non-Aeronautical Revenue Benchmarks: What the Best Airports Earn Per Passenger
waves.keywords: non-aeronautical revenue airports, airport commercial revenue per passenger, airport retail revenue benchmarks, spend per passenger airport
waves.brief: The SERP for non-aeronautical revenue is ACI's own blog, ScienceDirect, consultancies and report mills — no publisher at all, and this is the beat the title exists for. Write the benchmark explainer an airport commercial director would bookmark. Use ACI's published aggregates with attribution: non-aero was 73.3 billion dollars globally in 2024, around 37 percent of industry revenue, forecast 76 billion in 2025 and 99 billion by 2033; regional composition differs (parking 43.2 percent of non-aero in North America, retail 26.7 percent leading in Europe, retail 38.8 percent in Asia-Pacific and the Middle East). Explain the standard metrics: non-aero revenue per passenger, retail spend per head, penetration and dwell time, minimum annual guarantees versus revenue share. Pull real per-passenger figures from listed operators' published accounts where possible (Aena, Groupe ADP, Fraport publish commercial revenue lines; Avolta's 2024 revenue was 8.7 billion Swiss francs as the concessionaire-side scale marker) — every number named to its report and year. Explain what moves the number: passenger mix (transfer versus O and D, long-haul versus low-cost), terminal design and walk-through retail, digital pre-order, and the drop-off charge trend in the UK. Be honest that airports do not publish comparable per-passenger commercial figures uniformly, which is exactly why attributed benchmarks are valuable. This piece seeds the Non-Aero Revenue League franchise (brief section 8): write it so the annual update slots in.

waves.title: Airport Parking Revenue: The Quiet Profit Centre Worth 43 Percent of US Commercial Income
waves.keywords: airport parking revenue, airport car parking income, drop-off charges airport, airport parking business model, kiss and fly fees
waves.brief: A Substack ranks first for this query; no publisher owns it. Write the operator-side piece on parking as a revenue line. Anchor figures with attribution: parking is 24.1 percent of global airport non-aeronautical revenue per ACI, and 43.2 percent in North America where it is the biggest single commercial line; UK examples where published accounts allow (Manchester Airports Group's parking income has been reported around 190 million pounds a year — attribute to the accounts or the reporting, dated). Cover the models: airport-operated versus concession (APCOA, Q-Park, SP Plus), pre-book yield management (parking is the most price-managed product an airport sells), official versus off-site competition, and the drop-off charge phenomenon — the UK-specific kerb-side fee that the RAC surveys annually, now common at major UK airports and a recurring consumer-press story that we cover from the revenue side. Cover the threats honestly: ride-hailing and rail eating short-stay demand, EV charging as both cost and product, and autonomous-vehicle scenarios as a long-term structural question for a line many US airports depend on. Practical closer for operators: the levers that move parking yield (pre-book share, product tiers, dynamic pricing, enforcement). Tables with source lines throughout.

waves.title: What a Baggage Handling System Actually Costs, from Carousel to CT Screening
waves.keywords: baggage handling system cost, airport baggage system price, BHS cost per bag, baggage handling system suppliers, individual carrier system airport
waves.brief: The SERP is IATA, report mills, one local business journal and Beumer answering its own buyers' question — no independent publisher. Write the neutral cost explainer. Cover the system types and their cost character: conventional belt and pusher sortation, tilt-tray and cross-belt sorters, and individual carrier systems (ICS) at the top of the range; early bag storage; the hold-baggage screening integration that drives much of the cost (CT standard 3 machines and the conveyors that feed them). Name the supplier landscape neutrally: Vanderlande (Toyota Industries), Siemens Logistics, BEUMER Group, Daifuku, Alstef, Leonardo, Glidepath. Use published contract values as the cost evidence, each dated and attributed — for example Leonardo's reported 120 million dollar US baggage deal and other recent published awards from the wire — rather than asserting per-bag costs in our own voice; where industry rules of thumb exist (cost per metre of conveyor, cost per bag per hour of capacity), quote them as attributed ranges. Explain what drives cost beyond hardware: civils and the basement problem in retrofits, controls and software, redundancy requirements, and the operations and maintenance contract that often exceeds the capital cost over the system's life. Close with the procurement shape: how BHS tenders run, why airports increasingly buy availability rather than equipment.

waves.title: Airport Management Software: A Buyer's Guide to AODB, Ops and Resource Systems
waves.keywords: airport management software, AODB airport, airport operations software, airport resource management system, airport software vendors
waves.brief: A pure vendor SERP (Veoci, AeroCloud, altexsoft, ISO Gruppe, SafetyCulture) with no independent voice — a neutral buyer's guide becomes the only one. Explain the stack an operator actually buys: the AODB (airport operational database) as the core record of flights, stands, gates and belts; resource management systems that allocate them; A-CDM (airport collaborative decision making) and what Eurocontrol membership of it means; the passenger-processing layer (CUPPS, CUSS, biometrics orchestration); commercial systems (parking, concession, property) and the integration problem between all of them. Map the vendor landscape honestly by segment: SITA and Amadeus at the platform end, TAV Technologies, Veovo (Gentrack), INFORM, ADB Safegate's Beontra for planning, Assaia for apron AI, AeroCloud and similar cloud-native entrants at the regional-airport end. Comparison table: vendor, segment, deployment model, notable installs where published. Cover the buying questions that matter: cloud versus on-premise at an airport that cannot go down, integration with airline and ground-handler systems, per-turn versus licence pricing, and the small-airport trap of enterprise systems sized for hubs. Every vendor claim attributed to the vendor; no rankings asserted in our own voice.

waves.title: Airport Advertising: What the Space Is Worth and Who Runs It
waves.keywords: airport advertising rates, airport advertising revenue, airport advertising concession, JCDecaux airport, digital screens airport advertising
waves.brief: The current SERP is entirely media-buying agencies quoting their own rates — a neutral benchmark piece is unique on day one. Write it from the airport's side: advertising as a non-aero revenue line. Cover the concession model: JCDecaux Airport and Clear Channel Airports as the two global majors, plus oOh!media, APG|SGA and Intersection regionally; guarantee-plus-share deal shapes; contract lengths and what an airport should benchmark before tendering. Explain the inventory economics: why digital transformation multiplied yield per site (one screen, many campaigns), the premium sites (jet bridges, baggage hall, security trays, immigration corridor), programmatic entering airport out-of-home, and the audience argument agencies sell (dwell time, affluent demographics) presented as their claim, attributed. On rates: quote published agency rate-card ranges as attributed examples of what the market quotes rather than asserting our own, and note the airport's cut depends on the concession terms. Include the advertiser-side flip that makes this piece a shop window: airports themselves advertise (route development pitches to airlines, recruitment) — which is precisely this magazine's own commercial thesis. Close with tender-readiness questions for a commercial director.

Comparison table of the contenders on all three measures with source lines. This page becomes the standing reference we update when ACI's ranking drops each year.

waves.title: What an IT Outage Actually Costs an Airport
waves.keywords: airport IT outage cost, airport system failure, CrowdStrike airport cost, airport disruption cost, airport resilience
waves.brief: Tom's brief names this beat explicitly (what an IT outage or a snow day actually costs the place) and no publisher owns it. Build the piece on documented, attributed cases: the July 2024 CrowdStrike outage (Delta alone put the cost at 500 million dollars in its CEO's statement and around 550 million in filings, over 5,000 cancellations; quote both figures with their sources per the scope-and-figure rule; around 5.4 billion dollars estimated across the Fortune 500 per Parametrix, attributed), Heathrow and other baggage-system outages from the wire, and the March 2025 Heathrow substation fire closure as the power-resilience case (use the published inquiry figures; attribute). Structure the cost anatomy an ops director recognises: EU261 and refund liability, ground-handling overtime and hotel costs, aircraft and crew out of position, concession revenue lost with every cancelled departure, and the reputational and regulatory tail. Then the resilience procurement that follows every incident: uninterruptible power, failover for the AODB and departure control, manual fallback processes, and why airports now write recovery-time objectives into IT contracts. Close with the honest observation that resilience spend is unglamorous capex with a measurable payback, which is the argument an ops director takes to the board. Strictly no incident voyeurism: every case is a cost story, per the incident rule.

waves.title: E-Gates and Airport Biometrics: The Vendor Landscape and What Deployment Involves
waves.keywords: e-gates airport, airport biometrics, facial recognition airport, biometric boarding, EES e-gates Europe
waves.brief: The Points Guy owns the consumer news angle on this query; the winnable piece is the definitive operator-side explainer, which nobody has written. Cover the technology tiers: automated border control e-gates (the immigration layer, government-procured), biometric self-service touchpoints through the airport journey (bag drop, security, boarding), and the single-token architecture that links them. Map the vendor landscape: SITA, Idemia, NEC, Vision-Box (acquired by Amadeus in 2024 — attribute), Materna IPS, HID, CLEAR in the US membership model, Embross and Elenium at the kiosk layer. The live regulatory driver: the EU Entry/Exit System rollout and what it forces airports to deploy — cover status as of the drafting date with attribution, since EES timelines have moved repeatedly. Cover what deployment actually involves for an operator: the government/airport/airline three-way split of who pays and who owns the gallery, throughput per gate versus manned desks (quote vendor or trial figures as attributed claims), privacy and data-protection obligations stated neutrally, and the fallback problem when the system is down. A procurement-shaped comparison table: vendor, layer, notable deployments where published. No editorial position on surveillance politics per the geopolitics rule; report the operational and commercial case and the stated concerns, attributed.

waves.title: How Airports Win New Routes: Route Development, Incentives and the Pitch to Airlines
waves.keywords: airport route development, how airports attract airlines, airport route incentives, air service development, Routes conference
waves.brief: Route development is the one beat where airports are the advertiser rather than the audience target — Routes' entire event model is airports paying to pitch airlines — and the explainer SERP is thin (Routes' own content and consultancies). Write the neutral guide. Cover how the process works: the route-development team's case (catchment data, leakage analysis, yield forecasts), the pitch venues (Routes World — note it moved from Riyadh to Frankfurt for 2026, 21-23 October, with Fraport as official airport partner, attributed; Routes Europe; direct airline HQ meetings), and the consultancies that build the case (ASM, InterVISTAS, Landrum & Brown). Explain the incentive toolkit honestly and with the regulatory caveats: landing-charge discounts and growth rebates, marketing support funds, risk-sharing arrangements, and in Europe the state-aid rules that constrain public airports (attribute to the Commission's aviation guidelines; no legal advice in our own voice). Cover what airlines actually evaluate: aircraft availability, network fit, seasonality, and why most pitches fail — quote route-development practitioners' published commentary where available. Close with what a smaller airport can realistically do: data quality, one target carrier, patience measured in years. This piece establishes the beat the appointments and new-route wire queries then feed.
